q: What does OOP stand for?
options: Object-Oriented Programming
Object-Order Processing
Operation-Oriented Programming
Object-Only Programming
explanation: OOP stands for Object-Oriented Programming, a paradigm built around objects that bundle data and behavior.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four pillars of OOP?
options: Encapsulation
Inheritance
Compilation
Polymorphism
explanation: The four pillars are Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction. Compilation is a build step, not an OOP pillar.

q: In OOP, a "class" is best described as:
options: A blueprint for creating objects
A running instance of a program
A single value stored in memory
A type of loop
explanation: A class defines the structure and behavior that its objects (instances) will share.

q: An "object" is best described as:
options: A specific instance of a class with its own state
A synonym for a class
A function with no owner
A file on disk
explanation: An object is a concrete instance created from a class, holding its own attribute values.

q: Which of the following languages is NOT considered primarily object-oriented?
options: Java
Python
C
explanation: C is a procedural language with no built-in classes or objects, unlike Java, Python, and C++.

q: The main advantage of OOP over purely procedural code is:
options: Grouping related data and behavior together, improving modularity and reuse
Guaranteed faster execution in all cases
Removing the need for functions
Eliminating the need for variables
explanation: OOP bundles data with the operations on that data, which tends to improve modularity, reuse, and maintainability.

q: Smalltalk is historically significant in OOP because:
options: It was one of the first languages built around pure object messaging
It introduced the for-loop
It was the first functional language
It removed the need for classes
explanation: Smalltalk pioneered the idea that computation happens entirely through objects sending messages to each other.

q: In OOP terms, "state" refers to:
options: An object's current attribute/data values
The programming language's syntax
The compiler's internal settings
A method's return type
explanation: State is the data an object currently holds in its attributes/fields.

q: In OOP terms, "behavior" refers to:
options: The methods an object can perform
The object's memory address
The class's file name
The object's creation timestamp
explanation: Behavior is expressed through an object's methods — the actions it can take or respond to.

q: A "class attribute" (static field) differs from an instance attribute in that:
options: It is shared across all instances rather than unique per instance
It can only be an integer
It cannot be changed after class creation
It is always private
explanation: Class attributes live on the class itself and are shared by every instance unless an instance shadows them.

q: Which of these creates a new object of a class in Python?
options: Calling the class like a function, e.g., MyClass()
Using the keyword new MyClass
Writing MyClass::new()
Declaring var x: MyClass
explanation: Python creates instances by calling the class itself, e.g. obj = MyClass().

q: The term "object identity" refers to:
options: The unique reference distinguishing one object from another, even with equal data
The class name printed by str()
The object's hash value only
The order objects were created in a file
explanation: Identity is about which specific object you have, distinct from whether two objects happen to hold equal values.

q: Which of these is a good real-world analogy for a class?
options: A cookie cutter that produces many cookies
A single baked cookie
An oven timer
A grocery list
explanation: A class is a template (like a cookie cutter) used to stamp out many similar objects (cookies).

q: Which of these is a good real-world analogy for an object?
options: An individual cookie made from the cutter
The cutter itself
The recipe book
The kitchen
explanation: An object is one concrete instance produced from the class blueprint, just as one cookie comes from the cutter.

q: Why did OOP become popular for large-scale software in the 1990s?
options: It offered a natural way to model complex domains and manage growing codebases through modular, reusable components
It required less RAM than any other paradigm
It eliminated the need for testing
It was the only paradigm supporting graphics
explanation: As systems grew larger, OOP's modularity, encapsulation, and reuse made complex domains easier to manage than purely procedural code.

q: A "method" in OOP is:
options: A function defined inside a class that operates on its instances
A type of variable
A file extension
A loop construct
explanation: Methods are functions bound to a class, typically operating on that class's instances.

q: The "self"/"this" reference inside a method refers to:
options: The specific instance the method was called on
The class definition itself
The parent module
A global variable
explanation: self (Python) or this (Java/C++) points to the particular object the method is currently executing for.

q: Which of the following best defines a "constructor"?
options: A special method that initializes a newly created object
A method that deletes an object
A method that compares two objects
A method that only classes (not objects) can call
explanation: A constructor sets up a new object's initial state right after it is created.

q: What's the primary difference between a class and a module?
options: A class defines objects with state and identity; a module is just a namespace for grouping code
A module can be instantiated multiple times, a class cannot
A class has no methods, only data
There is no difference
explanation: Modules group related code under a namespace, while classes describe objects that carry their own state and identity.

q: Which pillar of OOP is concerned with hiding internal details?
options: Encapsulation
Inheritance
Polymorphism
Composition
explanation: Encapsulation bundles data with behavior and restricts direct access to internal details.

q: Which pillar of OOP is concerned with sharing behavior between related classes?
options: Inheritance
Encapsulation
Abstraction
Aggregation
explanation: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend a parent class's attributes and methods.

q: Which pillar of OOP lets one interface represent many underlying implementations?
options: Polymorphism
Encapsulation
Composition
Aggregation
explanation: Polymorphism allows the same operation/interface to behave differently depending on the concrete object.

q: Which pillar of OOP focuses on exposing only essential features while hiding complexity?
options: Abstraction
Inheritance
Encapsulation
Polymorphism
explanation: Abstraction simplifies interaction with a system by hiding unnecessary implementation complexity.

q: A "domain model" in OOP design usually refers to:
options: A set of classes mirroring real-world entities and their relationships in the problem being solved
A UML tool's file format
A database's index structure
A compiler optimization pass
explanation: A domain model represents the concepts, relationships, and rules of the problem domain using classes and objects.

q: Which of these best distinguishes procedural programming from OOP?
options: Procedural code centers on functions operating on separate data; OOP bundles data and functions into objects
Procedural code cannot use loops
OOP cannot use functions
Procedural programming was invented after OOP
explanation: In procedural programming, data and the functions acting on it are typically separate; OOP unifies them inside objects.

q:
What does the following Python code create?
class Car: pass
c = Car()
Code:
class Car: pass
c = Car()
options: An instance c of the empty class Car
A syntax error
A subclass of Car
Nothing, this code fails
explanation: class Car: pass defines an empty class; Car() then creates a new instance of it.

q:
What is the output of the following code?
Code:
class Counter:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self):
        Counter.count += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
print(Counter.count)
options: Error
explanation: count is a class attribute shared by all instances; each __init__ call increments it once, so after two instances it is 2.

q: Which special method in Python is called automatically right after an object is created, to initialize it?
options: __init__
__new__
__start__
__create__
explanation: __init__ runs immediately after object creation to set up the instance's initial attributes.

q: What happens if a class defines no __init__ method?
options: Python uses a default no-argument constructor that does nothing extra
The class cannot be instantiated
A compile-time error occurs
Python auto-generates all attributes as None
explanation: Without __init__, instances are created with no additional setup logic; you simply get a bare object.

q: How do you access an instance attribute named age from inside a method?
options: self.age
age
this->age
Car.age
explanation: Inside a Python instance method, attributes are accessed via self, e.g. self.age.

q: In Java, how do you create a new object of class Car?
options: Car c = new Car();
Car c = Car();
new c = Car();
Car.create();
explanation: Java requires the new keyword followed by a constructor call to allocate and initialize an object.

q: In C++, which keyword is used to allocate an object on the heap?
options: new
malloc only
heap
create
explanation: C++ uses the new operator to allocate objects dynamically on the heap.

q:
What is the output of the following code?
Code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

d1 = Dog("Rex")
d2 = Dog("Rex")
print(d1 == d2)
options: True
False
AttributeError
TypeError
explanation: Without a custom __eq__, Python's default equality compares object identity, and d1 and d2 are different objects.

q: Why does the previous example print False even though both dogs share the same name?
options: Python's default __eq__ compares object identity, not attribute values, unless overridden
Strings can never be compared with ==
Dog objects are automatically immutable
Python caches only the first created instance
explanation: Unless a class overrides __eq__, equality falls back to identity comparison (are they the same object in memory).

q: What is a "class method" typically used for?
options: Operations that relate to the class as a whole rather than one instance
Only converting types
Deleting instances
Storing private data
explanation: Class methods operate on the class itself (often via cls), useful for alternate constructors or class-wide operations.

q: Which decorator marks a Python method as a class method?
options: @classmethod
@staticmethod
@property
@abstractmethod
explanation: @classmethod marks a method to receive the class (cls) as its first argument instead of an instance.

q: What is the first parameter of a Python class method conventionally named?
options: cls
self
this
klass
explanation: By convention, class methods take cls as their first parameter, representing the class itself.

q: What is a "static method" in OOP?
options: A method that doesn't need access to instance or class state, grouped in a class for organization
A method that can never be called
A private constructor
A method that only runs once per program
explanation: Static methods behave like plain functions namespaced under a class, without needing self or cls.

q: Which decorator marks a Python method as static?
options: @staticmethod
@classmethod
@final
@override
explanation: @staticmethod removes the automatic self/cls binding, making the method behave like a plain function.

options: hi then hi
hi then Error
Error then hi
Error both times
explanation: A static method can be called on both the class and an instance, and behaves identically either way.

q: What does del obj do to an object in Python?
options: Removes the reference; the object is only destroyed once no references remain
Immediately frees the object's memory
Sets the object's attributes to None
Marks the class as deleted
explanation: del removes a name binding; the underlying object is only garbage-collected once its reference count hits zero.

q: Which of these correctly checks if x is an instance of class Foo?
options: isinstance(x, Foo)
type(x) is Foo only
x.instanceof(Foo)
Foo.check(x)
explanation: isinstance() is the idiomatic way to check an object's type, including subclasses.

q: What does type(x) == Foo check that isinstance(x, Foo) does not?
options: It requires x's exact type to be Foo, rejecting subclasses that isinstance would accept
It checks memory address equality
It is slower but otherwise identical
Nothing — they are always equivalent
explanation: type() gives the exact class; isinstance() also accepts subclasses, so the two can disagree for subclass instances.

q: In everyday OOP language, a class's "members" refers to:
options: Its attributes and methods collectively
Only its private fields
Only its public methods
Its subclasses
explanation: Members is a general term covering both the data (attributes) and behavior (methods) defined on a class.

q: What is the purpose of a "getter" method?
options: To provide controlled, read-only access to a private attribute
To delete an attribute
To create new classes dynamically
To convert an object to JSON
explanation: Getters expose a value to callers while letting the class control or validate how it's read.

q: What is the purpose of a "setter" method?
options: To provide controlled, validated write access to a private attribute
To read a value without side effects
To permanently lock an attribute
To rename a class
explanation: Setters let a class validate or transform incoming values before updating internal state.

q: What Python feature lets you define getters/setters accessed with plain attribute syntax (obj.value)?
options: The @property decorator
The @classmethod decorator
The __slots__ declaration
The @staticmethod decorator
explanation: @property lets a method be accessed like a plain attribute, while still running custom logic underneath.

q: What does class Dog(Animal): mean in Python?
options: Dog inherits from Animal
Dog and Animal are unrelated
Animal inherits from Dog
Dog is an alias for Animal
explanation: Placing a class name in parentheses after the class name declares it as the base (parent) class.

q: What's the difference between a class-body-level variable and one set via self.x in __init__?
options: The former is shared by instances until shadowed; the latter is unique per instance from the start
There is no difference
The former cannot be changed
The latter must be a constant
explanation: Class-level variables are shared until an instance assigns its own copy via self, which then shadows the class attribute for that instance.

q:
What is the output of the following code?
Code:
class A:
    items = []
    def add(self, x):
        self.items.append(x)

a = A()
b = A()
a.add(1)
print(b.items)
options: AttributeError
[None]
explanation: items is a mutable class attribute shared by all instances, so appending via one instance affects every instance.

q: Encapsulation primarily means:
options: Bundling data with the methods that operate on it and restricting direct outside access
Copying a class into another file
Running two threads at once
Compiling code ahead of time
explanation: Encapsulation packages an object's data with its behavior while limiting uncontrolled external access.

q: In Python, which naming convention signals a "protected" member by convention only?
options: Single leading underscore, e.g. _value
Double leading underscore, e.g. __value
ALL_CAPS naming
A trailing underscore, e.g. value_
explanation: A single leading underscore is a widely followed convention meaning "internal use", though it's not enforced by Python.

q: In Python, which naming convention triggers name mangling?
options: Double leading underscore, e.g. __value
Single leading underscore
A trailing double underscore, e.g. value__
Uppercase names
explanation: Names with two leading underscores (and at most one trailing) get mangled to _ClassName__value.

options: AttributeError
None
SyntaxError
explanation: __secret is name-mangled to _A__secret, so accessing it as __secret from outside raises AttributeError.

q: In Java, which access modifier restricts a member to only the declaring class?
options: private
public
protected
default (package-private)
explanation: private members are accessible only within the class where they're declared.

q: In Java, which access modifier allows access from any class?
options: public
private
protected
final
explanation: public members can be accessed from any code that can see the class.

q: In Java, protected access allows:
options: Access from the same package and from subclasses in other packages
Access only within the exact same class
Access from absolutely nowhere else
Access only from static contexts
explanation: protected is broader than package-private, additionally allowing subclasses outside the package to access the member.

q: In C++, members declared under private: are accessible:
options: Only within the class itself (and its friends)
From any subclass automatically
From any code in the same file
From any code that includes the header
explanation: C++ private members are restricted to the class itself, plus any explicitly declared friend functions/classes.

q: In C++, what does the friend keyword do?
options: Grants a specific external function or class access to another class's private members
Marks a function as thread-safe
Automatically generates getters and setters
Disables inheritance for that class
explanation: friend explicitly allows a chosen outside function or class to bypass normal access restrictions.

q: Why is direct public access to fields generally discouraged?
options: It removes the ability to validate or change internal representation later without breaking client code
It makes the program run slower
It prevents inheritance
It is illegal in most languages
explanation: Once a field is public, external code depends directly on it, making later changes to validation or representation risky.

q: A getter/setter pair around a field is sometimes criticized because:
options: It can just re-expose the field publicly without adding real validation or abstraction
It is always slower than direct field access
It cannot be used in Java
It prevents unit testing
explanation: Trivial getters/setters that simply pass values through provide little real encapsulation benefit over a public field.

q: What is "information hiding" as distinct from mere "access control"?
options: Hiding a class's implementation decisions so client code can't depend on them, even if access were technically possible
Making all variables global
Deleting unused code
Encrypting data at rest
explanation: Information hiding is a design discipline: even permitted access shouldn't be relied upon in ways that couple callers to internals.

q: Which of these is an example of a validated setter?
options: A method that only accepts a positive number and raises otherwise
A method that always returns None silently on bad input
A public field with no checks
A method that logs but still accepts anything
explanation: A validated setter enforces an invariant (like positivity) instead of blindly accepting any value.

q: What problem can arise if a class exposes a mutable internal list directly via a getter?
options: Callers can mutate the internal state from outside, bypassing any invariants the class tries to maintain
The list becomes immutable automatically
The getter will throw an exception
Nothing, this is always safe
explanation: Returning a reference to a mutable internal collection lets external code change it without going through the class's own methods.

q: What is a common fix for the mutable-internal-list exposure problem?
options: Return a copy of the list, or return a read-only/immutable view
Make the list a class attribute instead
Rename the getter method
Convert the list into a string
explanation: Returning a defensive copy or an immutable view prevents external code from altering internal state directly.

q: Encapsulation is most closely related to which design goal?
options: Reducing coupling by hiding internal implementation
Maximizing global variable usage
Improving numeric precision
Guaranteeing thread safety automatically
explanation: By hiding internals, encapsulation reduces how tightly other code is coupled to a class's implementation.

q: What does "tell, don't ask" encourage in encapsulated design?
options: Asking an object to perform an action rather than pulling out its internal data to act on it yourself
Always asking permission before calling any method
Never calling methods on other objects
Preferring global functions over methods
explanation: "Tell, don't ask" pushes behavior into the object that owns the relevant data, instead of extracting data to manipulate elsewhere.

q: Why might excessive getters and setters be considered an anti-pattern?
options: They can indicate that behavior which belongs inside the class has leaked out to callers
They always cause memory leaks
They are forbidden in modern Java
They make classes immutable
explanation: If a class is just a bag of getters/setters, the actual behavior often lives elsewhere, weakening true encapsulation.

q: In Python, is there a truly private (compiler-enforced) attribute?
options: No, Python relies on convention and name mangling rather than true enforcement
Yes, using the private keyword
Yes, but only inside dataclasses
Yes, if declared with __slots__
explanation: Python has no hard access-control keyword; privacy is a social convention reinforced by name mangling.

options: Balance becomes -50
Raises ValueError: Insufficient funds
Prints 100
Silently does nothing
explanation: The withdraw method validates the amount against the balance and raises ValueError when the withdrawal would overdraw the account.

q: What's the benefit of encapsulating validation logic inside a setter rather than scattering checks in calling code?
options: The invariant is enforced in exactly one place, no matter how many callers there are
It removes the need for testing
It makes the class immutable automatically
It is required by every programming language
explanation: Centralizing validation inside the class guarantees the rule is applied consistently everywhere the attribute is set.

q: Which of these best illustrates a broken encapsulation boundary?
options: A Rectangle class exposing width and height as public fields that other code multiplies directly instead of calling area()
A Rectangle class with a private width and a public area() method
A Rectangle class using a getter for width
A Rectangle class implementing __eq__
explanation: When external code recomputes logic (like area) using exposed raw fields instead of the class's own method, encapsulation has failed.

q: What is a "read-only property" used for?
options: Exposing a computed or internal value for reading without allowing external code to set it directly
Making an attribute writable by any code
Hiding a method entirely
Converting a method into a static method
explanation: A read-only property lets callers read a value through normal attribute syntax while blocking external writes.

q: In Python, how do you make an attribute readable via obj.value but raise an error if someone tries obj.value = x?
options: Define it with @property and don't define a matching setter
Use __slots__ = ['value']
Declare it as a class attribute only
Use @staticmethod on the getter
explanation: A @property without a corresponding @value.setter makes the attribute read-only from outside the class.

q: Encapsulation and abstraction are often confused; which best distinguishes them?
options: Encapsulation hides data/state, while abstraction hides implementation complexity behind a simpler interface
They are exactly the same concept
Encapsulation only applies to Java
Abstraction only applies to inheritance
explanation: Encapsulation protects internal state; abstraction simplifies what callers need to know about how something works.

q: Inheritance allows a class to:
options: Reuse and extend the attributes/methods of another class
Delete methods from unrelated classes
Convert itself into a function
Run on multiple threads automatically
explanation: Inheritance lets a subclass build on an existing class's behavior instead of rewriting it from scratch.

q: The class being inherited from is called the:
options: Base/parent/superclass
Child class
Interface only
Mixin
explanation: The class providing the shared behavior is called the base, parent, or superclass.

q: The class that inherits is called the:
options: Derived/child/subclass
Base class
Abstract class always
Static class
explanation: The class that extends another is the derived, child, or subclass.

q: What is "single inheritance"?
options: A class inherits from exactly one direct parent class
A class inherits from more than one parent
A class has only one method
A class cannot be subclassed further
explanation: Single inheritance restricts each class to one immediate superclass.

q: What is "multiple inheritance"?
options: A class inherits from more than one parent class directly
A class has multiple constructors
A class implements multiple interfaces only
A class is instantiated multiple times
explanation: Multiple inheritance allows a class to directly extend two or more parent classes.

q: Which of these languages supports multiple inheritance of classes directly?
options: Python (and C++), not Java
Java only
Neither Python nor Java
JavaScript only
explanation: Python and C++ allow a class to inherit from multiple classes directly; Java restricts classes to single inheritance.

q: Why doesn't Java allow multiple class inheritance?
options: To avoid the ambiguity of the diamond problem; Java uses interfaces instead
Because the JVM cannot execute more than one class file
Because Java has no concept of classes
Because it would make Java slower
explanation: Java sidesteps diamond-inheritance ambiguity by limiting classes to one parent, while allowing multiple interface implementation.

B
Error: ambiguous method
Both A and B
explanation: Python's MRO checks base classes left to right, so A's hello() is found before B's.

q: What does super() typically do in a subclass method?
options: Delegates to the parent class's version of that method
Deletes the parent class
Creates a totally new object
Converts the subclass into the parent class
explanation: super() gives access to the parent class's methods, commonly used to extend rather than fully replace behavior.

q: What is method "overriding"?
options: A subclass provides its own implementation of a method that already exists (same signature) in the parent
Defining two methods with the same name but different parameters
Deleting a parent method entirely
Renaming a method in the subclass
explanation: Overriding replaces the inherited implementation with the subclass's own version, used polymorphically at runtime.

q: In Java, which annotation is conventionally used to signal an intentional override?
options: @Override
@Overridden
@Inherit
@Super
explanation: @Override lets the compiler check that the method really does override a parent method, catching typos early.

q: If a subclass forgets to override a method correctly (e.g., typos the name), what typically happens?
options: A new, separate method is created rather than overriding, and dynamically typed languages may not flag it
A compiler error always occurs in every language
The parent method is automatically deleted
The program crashes immediately at import time
explanation: Without a signature/name match, the 'override' is really a new unrelated method; static languages with @Override catch this, dynamic ones may not.

q: Which of these best describes the "is-a" relationship created by inheritance?
options: A Car is-a Vehicle
A Car has-a Vehicle
A Car uses-a Vehicle
A Car creates-a Vehicle
explanation: Inheritance models an is-a relationship: a subclass is a more specific kind of its parent.

q: What does it mean for a method to be "final" (Java) or effectively non-overridable?
options: Subclasses cannot override or replace that method's implementation
The method can only be called once
The method is automatically static
The method has no return value
explanation: Marking a method final locks its implementation so subclasses cannot change its behavior.

q: Why is deep inheritance (many levels) often discouraged in modern design?
options: It tightly couples many classes together and makes changes to a base class risky and hard to trace
It is not supported by any language
It always causes a stack overflow
It automatically makes objects immutable
explanation: Long inheritance chains propagate changes unpredictably and make it hard to reason about behavior across many levels.

q: What is "constructor chaining" in inheritance?
options: A subclass constructor calling its parent's constructor before running its own logic
Creating multiple unrelated objects in sequence
Chaining method calls with dots
Calling a constructor from a static method
explanation: Constructor chaining ensures the parent's setup logic runs (often via super()) before the subclass adds its own.

q: In Python, if a subclass doesn't define __init__, what happens when you instantiate it?
options: The parent class's __init__ is used automatically
Instantiation fails
All attributes become None automatically
Python skips initialization entirely
explanation: Without its own __init__, a subclass inherits and uses its parent's __init__ unmodified.

Animal init
Dog init

Animal init

explanation: Once Dog overrides __init__, Animal's __init__ is not called automatically; only 'Dog init' prints.

q: To fix the previous example so both messages print, what should Dog.__init__ include?
options: A call to super().__init__() before or after its own print
A call to Animal() as a new object
A redefinition of Animal's class body
Nothing, it already works
explanation: Calling super().__init__() explicitly invokes the parent constructor's logic from within the subclass's constructor.

q: What is an "abstract base class" used for in an inheritance hierarchy?
options: Defining a common interface/contract that concrete subclasses must implement
Storing only private data
Preventing any subclassing at all
Making all methods static
explanation: Abstract base classes establish a shared contract, while leaving specific implementation details to concrete subclasses.

q: Why might you choose interface inheritance over implementation inheritance?
options: When you only want to share a contract/API, not any actual code, to keep coupling low
Because implementation inheritance is always faster
Because interfaces can hold private state
Because it removes the need for testing
explanation: Interface inheritance shares only method signatures, avoiding the tighter coupling that comes with inherited implementation.

q: What is the "fragile base class problem"?
options: A seemingly safe change to a base class silently breaks subclasses that depended on its previous internal behavior
A base class that has too few methods
A subclass that cannot be instantiated
A class hierarchy with no constructors
explanation: Because subclasses often rely on undocumented parent behavior, small parent changes can break them in unexpected ways.

q: Inheriting purely to reuse a few utility methods, without an actual is-a relationship, is generally considered:
options: A design smell — composition or a shared helper is usually better
Best practice in every case
Required by SOLID principles
Impossible in most languages
explanation: Using inheritance just for code reuse (without a true is-a relationship) often leads to awkward, tightly coupled designs.

q: What is a "sibling class" in an inheritance hierarchy?
options: Another subclass that shares the same immediate parent
The direct parent class
A class with no parent
A class in a completely unrelated hierarchy
explanation: Sibling classes both derive from the same parent but are not related to each other directly.

q: What algorithm does Python's MRO (Method Resolution Order) use?
options: C3 linearization
Depth-first search only
Breadth-first search only
Alphabetical ordering of class names
explanation: Python computes a deterministic method lookup order using the C3 linearization algorithm, visible via ClassName.__mro__.

q: Polymorphism means:
options: "Many forms" — the same operation behaving differently depending on the object it's invoked on
Having many constructors
Having many private fields
Compiling to many binaries
explanation: Polymorphism lets the same method call produce different behavior depending on the actual object type.

q: Which type of polymorphism is resolved at compile time via method overloading?
options: Static (ad-hoc) polymorphism
Dynamic (subtype) polymorphism
Runtime reflection
Duck typing
explanation: Overload resolution happens at compile time based on declared parameter types, known as static polymorphism.

q: Which type of polymorphism is resolved at runtime via method overriding?
options: Dynamic (subtype) polymorphism
Static (ad-hoc) polymorphism
Type erasure
Name mangling
explanation: Overriding is resolved dynamically, based on the actual object's runtime type, not its declared/static type.

q: Which of these is true about method overloading in Python?
options: Python doesn't support true overloading; a later same-named method definition replaces earlier ones
Python fully supports overloading by parameter type
Overloading in Python requires the @overload decorator to work at runtime
Python overloads automatically based on argument count only
explanation: Because Python is dynamically typed, defining multiple methods with the same name simply overwrites the previous definition.

q:

def greet(name):

    return f"Hi {title} {name}"

print(greet("Sam"))
options: Hi Sam
TypeError: missing required argument
Hi None Sam
SyntaxError
explanation: The second greet definition replaces the first, so calling greet with only one argument fails since title is required.

q: In Java, method overloading is distinguished by:
options: Different parameter lists (type, number, or order) for the same method name
Different return types only
Different access modifiers only
Different method bodies with identical signatures
explanation: Java resolves overloads based on the parameter list; return type or modifiers alone don't count.

q: Can two Java methods differ only by return type and be considered valid overloads?
options: No, return type alone is not sufficient to overload
Yes, always
Yes, but only for static methods
Yes, but only in interfaces
explanation: Java requires overloaded methods to differ in their parameter lists; return type alone causes a compile error.

q: What is "duck typing"?
options: Treating an object based on the methods/attributes it has, not its declared class
A strict compile-time type-checking system
A Python-only import mechanism
A form of static polymorphism unique to Java
explanation: Duck typing focuses on whether an object behaves as needed, rather than its formal type or class hierarchy.

q: Duck typing is most naturally associated with:
options: Dynamically typed languages like Python and Ruby
Statically typed languages like Java and C++
Assembly language
Database query languages
explanation: Dynamic languages check object capability at call time, making duck typing a natural fit.

q: Polymorphism lets you write code that:
options: Depends only on a shared interface rather than concrete implementation types
Only works with a single hardcoded class
Runs faster than any procedural alternative
Cannot use inheritance
explanation: Code written against a common interface can work with any object implementing that interface, regardless of exact type.

q: What is "parametric polymorphism"?
options: Writing a function/class that behaves generically over any type, e.g. a generic Stack<T>
Overloading operators like + and -
Overriding a base class method
Using reflection to inspect types
explanation: Parametric polymorphism (generics) lets code work uniformly across many types without rewriting it per type.

q: Which of these is an example of parametric polymorphism?
options: A generic List<T> in Java that can hold any type T
A method overloaded for int and double
An interface with default methods
A private helper method
explanation: Generic containers like List<T> are the classic example of parametric polymorphism.

q: What is "ad-hoc polymorphism" typically implemented via, besides overloading?
options: Operator overloading
Garbage collection
Reflection
Serialization
explanation: Operator overloading lets the same operator (like +) behave differently for different types, another form of ad-hoc polymorphism.

q: In Python, which magic method lets you overload the + operator for a custom class?
options: __add__
__plus__
__sum__
__concat__
explanation: Defining __add__ on a class customizes what the + operator does between instances of that class.

q: What is required for runtime (subtype) polymorphism via overriding?
options: The subclass method must have the same name/signature as the parent's virtual method
The subclass must define a new constructor
The parent class must be abstract
The method must be static
explanation: Overriding requires matching the parent's method signature so the call can be dispatched polymorphically at runtime.

q: In C++, what keyword must a base class method have for it to be overridden polymorphically via a base pointer?
options: virtual
override
abstract
dynamic
explanation: Marking a base method virtual enables dynamic dispatch through base class pointers/references in C++.

q: When calling shape->area() where shape is a Shape* pointing to a Circle, and area() is virtual, what determines which area() runs?
options: The actual runtime type of the object (Circle), not the pointer's declared type
The pointer's declared static type (Shape)
Whichever is compiled first
It is undefined behavior
explanation: Virtual dispatch resolves the call based on the object's real (dynamic) type at runtime, not the pointer's declared type.

q: What happens if a C++ base class method is NOT declared virtual and you call it through a base pointer to a derived object?
options: The base class's version runs regardless of the actual object type (static binding)
The derived class's version always runs
A compile error occurs
The program crashes
explanation: Without virtual, C++ resolves the call statically based on the pointer's declared type, ignoring the actual object's type.

q: Why is polymorphism useful when processing a mixed list of shapes (Circle, Square, Triangle)?
options: You can call shape.area() on each without checking its specific type
It automatically sorts the shapes by size
It prevents any of the shapes from being deleted
It converts all shapes into one type
explanation: Polymorphism lets uniform code (shape.area()) work correctly across every concrete shape type.

q: What anti-pattern does heavy reliance on chained isinstance checks to select behavior resemble?
options: Reimplementing polymorphism manually instead of using overriding, violating Open/Closed
A form of encapsulation
Standard use of the Strategy pattern
A performance optimization technique
explanation: Manually branching on type instead of using overriding usually means new types require editing existing code, violating OCP.

q: What is "covariant return typing" in polymorphism?
options: An overriding method may return a more specific subtype than the parent method's declared return type
A method that accepts any type as a parameter
A method with no return value
A method overloaded by return type
explanation: Covariant returns let an override narrow the return type safely, since callers expecting the parent type still get something compatible.

q: What is "contravariance" generally concerned with?
options: Allowing a more general (wider) parameter type in certain overriding/substitution contexts
Making all types identical
Removing type checking entirely
Sorting objects by type name
explanation: Contravariance permits accepting broader parameter types in specific substitution scenarios, the mirror of covariant returns.

q: Why can't Java freely allow contravariant parameter types in overrides?
options: A changed parameter type would create a new overload instead of a true override, breaking substitutability
Java forbids all parameters in overrides
It would make the JVM crash
Java doesn't support parameters at all
explanation: Widening a parameter type in Java results in an overload, not an override, since Java doesn't support parameter contravariance for overriding.

q: What is "double dispatch" and why can't a single virtual call achieve it alone?
options: Behavior depends on the runtime types of two objects; single dispatch only resolves based on one receiver
It means calling a method twice for reliability
It refers to sending the same message to two different objects
It is a synonym for method overloading
explanation: A single virtual call dispatches only on the receiver's type, so patterns like Visitor chain two calls to react to two objects' types.

q: Abstraction in OOP means:
options: Exposing only essential features/behavior while hiding implementation complexity
Making all class members public
Removing all comments from code
Converting classes into functions
explanation: Abstraction lets users interact with a simplified interface without needing to understand the underlying complexity.

q: Which of these best illustrates abstraction?
options: A car's steering wheel and pedals hide the mechanical complexity underneath
A car's engine block diagram
A list of every bolt in a car
The car's full assembly manual
explanation: Drivers interact with a simple interface (wheel, pedals) without needing to understand the engine's internals.

q: An abstract class differs from a fully concrete class in that:
options: It cannot be instantiated directly and may leave some methods unimplemented
It cannot have any methods at all
It must be the top of every hierarchy
It cannot have a constructor
explanation: Abstract classes exist to be extended; some or all of their methods may lack implementations until subclassed.

q: Can an abstract class have both abstract and concrete (fully implemented) methods?
options: Yes
No, only abstract methods are allowed
No, only concrete methods are allowed
Only in Python, not in Java
explanation: Abstract classes can mix implemented (shared) methods with abstract ones that subclasses must fill in.

q: Can you instantiate an interface directly in Java?
options: No, interfaces cannot be instantiated directly
Yes, always
Yes, but only static interfaces
Only if it has default methods
explanation: Interfaces declare a contract without a concrete implementation, so they cannot be instantiated on their own.

q: What must a concrete subclass of an abstract class do?
options: Implement all of its inherited abstract methods
Redefine every method, even non-abstract ones
Remove the parent class's constructor
Convert itself into an interface
explanation: To become instantiable, a subclass must provide implementations for every abstract method it inherits.

TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Circle with abstract method area
Prints 0
SyntaxError
explanation: Circle inherits Shape's abstract method area() without implementing it, so Python refuses to instantiate it.

q: What's the key structural difference between an abstract class and a classic interface?
options: An abstract class can hold shared state and implemented methods; a classic interface only declares a contract
An interface can be instantiated, an abstract class cannot
Abstract classes cannot have any methods
There is no structural difference
explanation: Abstract classes may carry both state and behavior; a classic interface traditionally offers only method signatures.

q: Which of these is a benefit of programming to an abstraction rather than a concrete class?
options: Implementations can be swapped without changing the code that depends on the abstraction
It guarantees the code runs faster
It removes the need for any interface at all
It prevents subclassing entirely
explanation: Depending on an abstraction decouples client code from any single concrete implementation, easing future changes.

q: Since Java 8, interfaces can include:
options: default methods with a body, not just abstract method signatures
private constructors
instance fields with mutable state
final classes nested automatically
explanation: Java 8 introduced default methods, letting interfaces provide a body while still allowing implementers to override it.

q: What problem do "default methods" in Java interfaces solve?
options: They let an interface add new methods without breaking every existing implementing class
They make interfaces instantiable
They remove the need for abstract classes entirely
They allow multiple inheritance of state
explanation: Default methods provide a fallback implementation so older implementing classes don't break when an interface gains new methods.

q: What is a common analogy for abstraction in software?
options: A TV remote's buttons abstract away the circuitry that changes the channel
A spreadsheet's raw binary file format
A CPU's transistor layout
A network cable's physical wiring
explanation: Users press a simple button without needing to understand the internal electronics that make the channel change happen.

q: What does it mean to say abstraction reduces "cognitive load"?
options: Users of a class only need to understand its public interface, not its internal workings
It makes code compile faster
It reduces the number of classes needed to zero
It eliminates the need for documentation
explanation: A clean abstraction lets users reason about what a class does without tracking every implementation detail.

q: Which of these is NOT typically part of a well-designed abstraction?
options: Exposing every internal helper method publicly
A small, focused public interface
Hiding unnecessary implementation details
Clear method names describing intent
explanation: Exposing every internal helper defeats the purpose of abstraction by revealing implementation details unnecessarily.

q: What is a "pure virtual function" in C++?
options: A virtual function with no implementation in the base class, declared with = 0, forcing derived classes to implement it
A function that can never be overridden
A function that runs at compile time only
A function accessible from any namespace
explanation: Declaring a virtual function as = 0 makes it pure virtual, requiring any concrete subclass to supply an implementation.

q: In C++, a class containing at least one pure virtual function is called:
options: An abstract class, and cannot be instantiated
A final class
A template class
A friend class
explanation: Any class with an unimplemented pure virtual function becomes abstract in C++ and cannot be instantiated directly.

q: What is the purpose of a "protocol" in Python's typing system (PEP 544)?
options: To define structural typing — a set of methods a class must have, without requiring explicit inheritance
To enforce private access at runtime
To replace all classes with functions
To generate documentation automatically
explanation: Protocols check whether an object has the right shape (methods/attributes), independent of its class hierarchy.

q: How does a Protocol differ from an ABC in Python regarding subclassing?
options: A class satisfies a Protocol just by having matching methods (structural), while an ABC typically requires explicit inheritance (nominal)
Protocols require explicit inheritance, ABCs do not
Both require identical syntax and behave the same
Protocols can only be used with dataclasses
explanation: Protocols use structural typing (duck typing checked statically); ABCs use nominal typing based on declared inheritance.

q: Which principle says clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces/methods they don't use?
options: Interface Segregation Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Open/Closed Principle
Liskov Substitution Principle
explanation: ISP encourages splitting large interfaces into smaller, more focused ones tailored to each client's needs.

q: Why is a giant, all-encompassing interface (a "fat interface") a poor abstraction?
options: It forces unrelated implementers to provide methods irrelevant to them, increasing coupling
It compiles slower than smaller interfaces in every language
It cannot be implemented by more than one class
It is automatically insecure
explanation: A fat interface bundles unrelated responsibilities, forcing implementers to support methods that don't apply to them.

q: What's the relationship between abstraction and API design?
options: A good API is essentially a well-chosen abstraction over an implementation's complexity
APIs and abstraction are unrelated concepts
APIs must always expose full implementation details
Abstraction only applies to internal code, never public APIs
explanation: Designing a good API means choosing what complexity to hide and what simple contract to expose to callers.

q: Which of these questions best tests whether an abstraction is well-designed?
options: Can callers use it correctly without knowing how it's implemented internally?
Does it have the maximum possible number of public methods?
Is every internal variable exposed for flexibility?
Does it avoid using any interfaces?
explanation: A good abstraction lets callers use it correctly based on its documented contract alone, without peeking inside.

q: What is a "leaky abstraction"?
options: An abstraction that fails to fully hide its underlying implementation details, forcing callers to understand them anyway
An abstraction with too few public methods
A class with a memory leak
An interface with no implementers
explanation: A leaky abstraction requires callers to understand underlying details it was supposed to hide, undermining its purpose.

q: Give an example of a leaky abstraction.
options: A cloud storage API that behaves like a local filesystem, but callers must still handle network latency and partial failures
A Stack class with push and pop methods only
A Shape interface with an area() method
A private helper method inside a class
explanation: Network-backed APIs that pretend to be simple local resources still expose failure modes unique to networking, leaking the abstraction.

q: True or false: abstraction is only relevant to statically typed languages.
options: False — abstraction is a design concept, applicable in any OOP language
True — dynamic languages cannot express abstraction
True — only Java and C++ support abstraction
False, but only Python supports it
explanation: Abstraction is a design principle that applies regardless of whether a language is statically or dynamically typed.

q: What is the purpose of Python's __init__ method?
options: To initialize a newly created object's attributes
To create the raw object in memory
To delete an object
To compare two objects
explanation: __init__ runs right after object creation to set up the instance's starting attribute values.

q: What is the purpose of Python's __new__ method?
options: To actually create and return the new instance, before __init__ initializes it
To finalize garbage collection
To define class-level constants
To register the class with the interpreter
explanation: __new__ is responsible for allocating and returning the object itself; __init__ then configures it.

q: Which magic method controls the output of len(obj)?
options: __len__
__size__
__count__
__length__
explanation: Defining __len__ lets built-in len() work with a custom class.

q: Which magic method allows an object to be used with the in operator (membership testing)?
options: __contains__
__has__
__member__
__includes__
explanation: __contains__ customizes what x in obj checks for a custom class.

q: Which magic method allows indexing syntax like obj[0]?
options: __getitem__
__index__
__get__
__slice__
explanation: __getitem__ lets a custom object support square-bracket indexing.

q: Which magic method lets an object be called like a function, e.g., obj()?
options: __call__
__invoke__
__run__
__exec__
explanation: Defining __call__ makes instances of a class callable just like functions.

q: Which magic method controls how an object behaves in a boolean context (if obj:)?
options: __bool__
__truth__
__cond__
explanation: __bool__ defines what truthy/falsy value an object has when evaluated in a condition.

q:

print(bool(e))
options: True
False
TypeError
None

q: What do __enter__ and __exit__ together implement?
options: The context manager protocol used by the with statement
The iterator protocol
Operator overloading for +
Custom string formatting
explanation: These two methods define setup and teardown behavior for objects used with Python's with statement.

q: What does __iter__ need to return for an object to be iterable?
options: An iterator object (often self, if the class also defines __next__)
A list of all attribute names
The class itself, unconditionally
Nothing — it can return None
explanation: __iter__ must return an iterator, which is commonly the object itself when __next__ is also implemented.

q: Which exception should __next__ raise to signal the end of iteration?
options: StopIteration
IndexError
EOFError
KeyError
explanation: Raising StopIteration is the standard protocol for signaling that an iterator has no more items.

q: Why must __hash__ and __eq__ be defined consistently?
options: Two objects considered equal by __eq__ must produce the same hash, or they will behave incorrectly in sets/dicts
Python requires both to return the same numeric type
Hashing is unrelated to equality in Python
__hash__ must always return 0 for custom classes
explanation: Sets and dicts rely on equal objects hashing identically; violating this breaks lookups and membership tests.

q: If a class defines __eq__ but not __hash__ in Python, what happens by default?
options: The class becomes unhashable (instances can't be used in sets or as dict keys)
Nothing changes at all
Python auto-generates a matching __hash__
A SyntaxError occurs immediately
explanation: Python sets __hash__ to None automatically when __eq__ is defined without __hash__, making instances unhashable.

q: Which magic method customizes what + does between two custom objects?
options: __add__
__plus__
__sum__
__combine__
explanation: __add__ is invoked when the + operator is used with an instance of the class on the left side.
